title: Viktor: AI Coworker That Lives in Slack — Fryderyk Wiatrowski

primary.label: Agent Architecture & Harnesses

domains.label: General Purpose
domains.rationale: The talk centers on product design, user trust, model personality, and human collaboration with an AI coworker, with agent architecture details discussed in service of the product experience. Viktor serves internal enterprise workflows and knowledge work in companies while also functioning as an individual productivity assistant accessed through Slack. Viktor launched in February with real enterprise customers, demonstrated product-market fit, and is actively deployed in production. The talk is accessible to a general audience but covers intermediate concepts like memory isolation, context leakage, and interaction-mode mapping. This is a conference presentation by Viktor's co-founder at the AI Engineer channel describing product lessons and company journey. All evidence anchors are directly stated in the transcript with grade said_in_transcript and no external verification.

summary: Frederick introduces Viktor as an AI employee living in Slack—no web UI, participating in channels and threads like a human teammate. Launched in February with zero expectations, it achieved immediate product-market fit and worldwide adoption. Viktor has access to 3,000 integrations, inherits integrations from whoever connects them first, giving the whole team access without repeated setup. Unlike human employees, Viktor has horizontal context across all company areas. The company's journey began in 2023 with browser-based AI agents (JCAI), state-of-the-art on WebArena but unreliable—3 to 5 steps at 60% reliability, compounding with each step. After Sonnet 3.5, they built Jace, an email-triggered agent that could react with tool calls such as automatic refunds. In February, they launched Viktor as a company agent, distinct from personal agents: one person connects integrations and the entire team inherits access. Scaling from personal to company agent introduces major challenges. Memory clutter accelerates 100x with 100 users. Context from growth channels must not leak into engineering or support channels, and DMs must stay private. Slack was chosen because it makes Viktor feel human and reframes 10-minute task latency as fast. Slack's multiple interaction modes—DMs, threads, emoji reactions, edits, deletions—must all map into linear context. Thread abandonment requires rolling over previous conversation context. Model personality matters as much as capability: users raged when Opus 4.6 was A/B tested against cheaper GPT 5.4. Viktor can proactively join conversations—for example, checking PostHog to verify statistical significance of A/B test claims—but proactive behavior on day one can alarm security teams, so rollout should be gradual. Viktor differs from desktop agents like Claude Code by working in the cloud without requiring your computer open, and its shared-context model means one person's integration connection serves the whole team. A customer story illustrates the 'not a tool, a hire' philosophy: an admin connected a personal Gmail, and the team started querying his emails, prompting Viktor to add integration scoping for personal versus shared connections. Frederick concludes with three pillars for a great AI coworker: helps get work done, knows the company via Slack context, and is friendly. He frames this within a historical arc from Leibniz's 17th-century vision of automating calculation to today's potential to automate all cognitive tasks, and offers the audience $100 in free credits to try Viktor.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

sections.title: Introduction to Viktor
sections.summary: Frederick introduces Viktor as an AI employee in Slack with no web UI. It participates in channels and threads like a teammate, has access to 3,000 integrations, can build its own connections, and has broad horizontal context across all company areas—unlike human employees who have narrow domain expertise.

sections.title: Company History: JCAI to Jace to Viktor
sections.summary: The company started in 2023 building browser-based AI agents (JCAI), which was state-of-the-art on WebArena but unreliable at 3-5 steps with 60% reliability. After Sonnet 3.5, they built Jace, an email-triggered agent that could react with tool calls like automatic refunds. In February they launched Viktor, the company agent in Slack.

sections.title: Company Agent vs Personal Agent
sections.summary: Viktor differs from personal agents like Open Claw: one person connects integrations and the whole team inherits access, eliminating 100x repeated setup. This model introduces challenges around memory and access control that personal agents don't face.

sections.title: Memory Isolation Challenges
sections.summary: With 100 users, memory clutter occurs 100x faster. Context from growth channels must not leak into engineering or support channels. DMs must remain private. The same agent needs channel-specific context isolation while serving the entire company.

sections.title: Why Slack as Interface
sections.summary: Slack was chosen for two reasons: it makes Viktor feel like a human employee (you don't interact with coworkers in web apps), and it reframes 10-minute task latency as fast—shocking compared to normal Slack response expectations, versus frustrating in a web app where you wait staring at a screen.

sections.title: What Breaks in Slack: Interaction Modes, Tone, and Proactivity
sections.summary: Slack's multiple interaction modes—DMs, threads, emoji reactions, edits, deletions—must all map into linear context. Thread abandonment requires rolling over previous conversation context. Model personality matters: users raged when Opus 4.6 was A/B tested against cheaper GPT 5.4. Viktor also proactively suggests workflow automations by monitoring channel conversations.

sections.title: Proactive Behavior Risks, Shared Context, and Integration Scoping
sections.summary: Proactive behavior can alarm security teams if Viktor starts DMing everyone on day one; gradual rollout is recommended. Viktor differs from desktop agents like Claude Code by running in the cloud. Shared context means one person's integration serves the whole team (e.g., 20-person growth team in a 100-person company). A customer story: an e-commerce brand admin connected personal Gmail as a team integration, exposing his emails to the team—prompting Viktor to add integration scoping for personal vs shared connections.

sections.title: Three Pillars, Vision, and Call to Action
sections.summary: Frederick summarizes three pillars for a great AI coworker: helps get work done (models are capable, connect via Pipedream), knows the company (context from Slack, requires Slack approval process), and is friendly (team and agent should like each other). He frames this within Leibniz's 17th-century vision of automating calculation, extending to all cognitive tasks today, and offers attendees $100 in free Viktor credits.
